name: Tensho
description: The soft counterpart to Sanchin, with flowing circular movements and open-hand techniques.

origin.title: Origin
origin.content: Tensho is a kata that Chōjun Miyagi himself developed after his return from China (ca. 1916–1921). He called it a "soft Sanchin". In 1921, Miyagi formulated the kata as the Yin counterpart to the hard, linear Sanchin. Tensho was intended to highlight the soft side (sōsō = yin) of the Naha-ki revelation. The kata would be partly derived from Southern Chinese Kung Fu forms such as Rokishu ("six hand functions") or from White Crane/Monk Fist traditions, but the fact is that Miyagi presented the specific flowing hand movements as his own creation within Goju. He saw Tensho as an exercise in soft, circular energy exercises.

transmission.title: Transmission to Goju-Ryu
transmission.content: Tensho was immediately spread among Miyagi's students after creation. It is taught in all Goju-ryu styles as the second kata (the second Sanchin) for black belt candidates. Other styles also adopted Tensho: Mas Oyama placed Tensho (he called it Tenchi Katas) in Kyokushin's curriculum as an example of a "southern kata". In short, the kata remained exclusively Goju in core (via Miyagi → Morio Higaonna etc.), but also found followers in the broader karate school via Gogen Yamaguchi and Oyama.

historicalDevelopment.title: Historical Development
historicalDevelopment.content: Tensho is historically closely related to Sanchin. It has no major external variations (it was already a new addition in 1921). However, some Goju schools introduce slightly different breathing frameworks (respiration schemes) and much attention is paid to finger arrangement (such as 'rotating' the palms). Over the years, however, Tensho has remained extremely consistent. In Kyokushin, the kata (with some tempo adjustments) stems directly from Oyama's Goju instruction. The "hardness" of the kata remains relatively mild; the emphasis is on fluidity under muscle tension.

technicalFeatures.title: Technical and Philosophical Characteristics
technicalFeatures.content: Tensho is known for its flowing, circular movements and soft hand forms. Each movement is performed under tension while energy rotates in the palms. Characteristic are the tensho (rotating palm blocks), various open-hand 'weave' and 'roof' blocks (tate- and yoko-koken), and related to this the use of index finger and thumb tips for consolidation. Breathing is used deeply and controlled to power the flowing movements. Philosophically, Tensho emphasizes refinement and internal energy (qi); Miyagi described it as an exercise in perfection and concentration. Practically, Tensho teaches the body to move smoothly with tension in it, and to consciously "walk with energy" in one's own hands.

controversy.title: Controversy/Variations within Goju-Ryu
controversy.content: In its own nature, Tensho is not a source of disagreement: it is clearly a Miyagi creation. Differences arise only through interpretation: some schools emphasize extra ibuki grips, others the change of hand openings. In Japan, where JKF Goju Kai / Jundokan work from Higaonna's Goju, the same precise version is usually maintained. Tensho is less controversial than, for example, Sanseiru. Any "competition" variant comes from Kyokushin, but that is secondary for Goju.

relationships.title: Relationship to Other Kata/Systems
relationships.content: Tensho is explicitly the Yin variant of Sanchin. Where Sanchin is the hard linear approach, Tensho is the soft, circular approach within the same principle (hard-soft taijutsu). There are also parallels with Chinese Rokushu and Monk forms: based on Yuán-ling (monk palm) and Baihequan (white crane), which called for added theories about "monk palms" in Tensho. Furthermore, Tensho was seen in Kyokushin as a typical southern kata (via Oyama), which embedded it in the entire karate community. Tensho and Sanchin thus form a pair that only occurs in systems that go through Goju.

modernPractice.title: Use in Modern Practice
modernPractice.content: Tensho is one of the standard kata in Goju-ryu, often as the second kata after Gekisai's for advanced students. It is used extensively for breathing and concentration training. Tensho can also appear in competitions (kata competitions or kata-shiai) due to its graceful execution. In the dojo, Tensho is emphasized for its health benefits and energy training (like the saying "A Tensho per day…"). It is beloved for its beautiful form and to teach young instructors how a kata can also be powerful without hard contact grips. In short, Tensho remains a cornerstone in lesson plans, as a counterweight to Sanchin and as a learning tool for technical finesse.

nameAndMeaning.title: Name and Meaning
nameAndMeaning.content: Tensho (転掌) means "rotating or revolving palms". The characters 転 (ten) and 掌 (shō) stand for "rotate/transition" and "palm". Literally you would translate it as "rotated palm"; a representation of the flow of open-hand movements in the kata. The name describes the swinging hand techniques that characterize the kata.
